title: Concurrent training: a meta-analysis examining interference of aerobic and resistance exercises
authors: Wilson JM, Marin PJ, Rhea MR, Wilson SM, Loenneke JP, Anderson JC
journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
population: 21 studies (422 effect sizes) comparing strength training alone, endurance training alone and concurrent training; population not described in the abstract
findings: Mean ES for hypertrophy: strength alone 1.23, endurance alone 0.27, concurrent 0.85. Strength: 1.76, 0.78 and 1.44. Power: 0.91, 0.11 and 0.55 (all three groups significantly different for power).
Resistance training concurrent with running, but not cycling, produced significant decrements in hypertrophy and strength.
Endurance training frequency (r -0.26 to -0.35) and duration (r -0.29 to -0.75) correlated negatively with hypertrophy, strength and power gains.
Authors conclude that interference is a factor of the modality, frequency and duration of the endurance training selected.
limitations: Pre-2012 literature; correlational moderator analyses with several effect sizes per study; outcomes are strength, hypertrophy and power, not running performance or economy; later and larger meta-analyses (Schumann 2022) found less interference for maximal strength and hypertrophy.
implications: Do not stack heavy or explosive sessions directly onto long or high-volume running days.
At peak endurance volume, plan lifting at maintenance volume and expect smaller strength gains; this is a plausible management rule, not a proven threshold.
Use as a counterweight to Schumann 2022: interference is most credible for power development at high endurance volume.
